sections.overview: Anartia amathea is a Neotropical brush-footed butterfly ranging from Central America through much of South America and several Caribbean islands. It is often seen in open and disturbed places as well as forest edges.
sections.identification: The upper wings are dark brown to black with red-orange patches and a band of white spots; the underside repeats the pattern more softly. Males are usually vivid red, while females tend toward orange and are somewhat larger. The Trinidad guide gives an approximate 4 cm wingspan, not a separate male/female range.
sections.habitat: Adults use sunny clearings, fields, pastures, gardens and river margins, including disturbed land and secondary growth. Records extend from low elevations to about 1,600 m in parts of its range.
sections.diet: Adults drink nectar from flowering plants. Caterpillars feed on host foliage; documented hosts include Acanthaceae, but the full host-plant list remains incomplete.
sections.behavior: It is active by day; adults may shelter, feed and mate in the same local areas, but the Trinidad guide reports no structured groups.
sections.reproduction: Females lay greenish eggs on host plants; one Trinidad account reports several hundred and a potential total near 800.
sections.ecology: Its caterpillars depend on suitable host plants, while nectar-feeding adults use flowering vegetation in open landscapes. Red and orange wing patches differ between sexes and make the butterfly conspicuous in flight.
sections.conservation: The species is reported as common in disturbed settings across a broad Neotropical range, but the consulted accounts provide no quantitative population trend.
